job.style: a short story with Indian characters in everyday life

passage: Rohan and his grandfather sat on their balcony in Jaipur, watching the sunset. Rohan pointed at the rooftop solar panels installed last year. 'Grandpa, since the sun is setting, will the panels stop working and start storing power for the night?' he asked. His grandfather smiled, 'Actually, Rohan, solar panels convert sunlight directly into electricity using the photovoltaic effect, not by heating water. When the sun goes down, they stop producing power immediately. We rely on the grid or batteries to bridge that gap because solar energy is intermittent.' Rohan looked at his father’s new electric car charging in the driveway. 'Is that car burning fuel to run?' he asked. His father laughed, 'No, it uses a battery-powered motor, not an engine that burns fuel. However, the true environmental benefit depends on whether the electricity charging it comes from coal or clean sources like wind and solar.' They discussed how India is rapidly expanding its renewable capacity, including wind farms in coastal areas where winds are strong and consistent. 'We cannot just put wind turbines anywhere,' his grandfather explained. 'They need specific locations to be effective. Also, we must remember that fossil fuels like coal take millions of years to form, so they are non-renewable, unlike the constant energy we harness from the sun and wind.'

items.evidence: When the sun goes down, they stop producing power immediately.
items.q: After sunset, a house has solar panels but no grid or battery. What happens to its solar power?
options: It stops, because panels need sunlight to make power
It continues, because good panels make power at night
It continues, because stored heat keeps turning turbines
It stops, because cool evening air blocks the panels
items.explain: Panels turn sunlight into electricity, so they stop producing power as soon as the sun goes down.

wrong.why: thinks a good panel gives power at night
thinks panels trap heat to run turbines
thinks cool air, not missing sunlight, stops panels

items.evidence: We rely on the grid or batteries to bridge that gap because solar energy is intermittent.
items.q: Why does the family still depend on the grid or batteries?
options: Solar power is not steady, so gaps need cover
Solar power is only for one house, never the grid
Solar power fails in cool weather, so backup helps
Solar power vanishes on cloudy days, so backup helps
items.explain: Solar energy is intermittent, so the grid or batteries must fill the gaps when panels stop producing.

wrong.why: thinks rooftop power can never reach the grid
thinks cloudy days give no power

items.evidence: However, the true environmental benefit depends on whether the electricity charging it comes from coal or clean sources like wind and solar.
items.q: Why might an electric car still harm the environment?
options: Its charging power may come from burning coal
Its motor still burns some fuel to run
Its clean power sources always damage nature
Its battery cannot be charged from solar power
items.explain: The car's benefit depends on its electricity source; power made from coal can still pollute.

wrong.why: thinks an electric car burns fuel like an engine
thinks all clean energy harms nature
thinks wind and solar cannot charge cars

items.evidence: They discussed how India is rapidly expanding its renewable capacity, including wind farms in coastal areas where winds are strong and consistent.
items.q: Why are wind farms placed at chosen sites instead of everywhere in India?
options: Only some sites have strong, steady winds
Turbines need hot weather, which coasts always have
Forests are the only land they may use
Coasts are cheaper, though any wind gives equal power
items.explain: Wind farms go where winds are strong and consistent, so site matters for the power they give.

wrong.why: mixes up weather needs of solar and wind
thinks energy projects only take forest land
thinks any site gives the same wind power

items.evidence: Also, we must remember that fossil fuels like coal take millions of years to form, so they are non-renewable, unlike the constant energy we harness from the sun and wind.
items.q: Why can't nature replace used coal within a few years?
options: Nature needs millions of years to form more
Nature renews coal as quickly as it renews wind
Sunlight and wind slowly change into new coal
Burning coal slowly returns it to the ground
items.explain: Coal takes millions of years to form, so it is non-renewable, unlike sun and wind energy.

wrong.why: mixes coal's origin with renewable sources
thinks used coal returns to the ground
